It reports no heart events or rhythm findings, cannot say whether the heart-rate rise came from the extra cocaine or from cocaethylene, and cannot show what happens outside a ward. In a second double-blind laboratory study, 10 adults who used cocaine and alcohol (8 men and 2 women, mean age 34, none of whom had sought treatment for cocaine problems) drank alcohol (1 g per kg) an hour before cocaine was infused into a vein over 15 minutes, in four sessions with labelled cocaine at 0.3, 0.6 or 1.2 mg per kg or a cocaine placebo and one double-placebo session (study conditions, not amounts to use): about 17% of the cocaine dose (SD 6) appeared as cocaethylene, in the same proportion across the four-fold dose range, and cocaethylene peaked later than cocaine and at far lower levels (16.8 to 53.1 against 250 to 891 ng/mL). None was found when cocaine was given without alcohol. With alcohol present, less benzoylecgonine, the breakdown product urine tests look for, was formed and excreted (peak blood level 69% and urine concentration about half of the cocaine-alone values). In those sessions, unlike the intranasal studies, alcohol did not raise cocaine exposure: in the 6 people who later also had a cocaine-alone session, cocaine exposure over the session and its peak did not differ, although cocaine's half-life was longer with alcohol (1.91 against 1.29 hours), and they rated drug liking and total intoxication higher across time, but not at their peak, with alcohol than with cocaine alone. That cocaine-alone session was neither blinded nor randomized and came 1 to 3 months later, in 6 of the 10 people, and a tracer dose of labelled cocaethylene was given in every session, so no session was free of cocaethylene (Harris et al., 2003). When cocaethylene itself was infused into a vein at the same doses as cocaine (0.25 and 0.5 mg per kg) in 6 adults with cocaine dependence who also met criteria for alcohol abuse or dependence, each taking all five conditions double-blind with placebo, it raised heart rate less than cocaine and produced lower ratings of cocaine high, any high, rush and feeling stimulated, while systolic blood pressure rose about equally in all four active conditions and diastolic pressure showed no difference; cocaethylene was cleared more slowly (half-life about 146 to 149 against 87 to 91 minutes). The lower dose of each drug was always given before the higher one, so dose and session order are mixed together, and the blind held poorly at the lower doses: given cocaine at 0.25 mg per kg, 5 of the 6 said they had been given cocaethylene (Hart et al., 2000). Cocaethylene is found in people's blood after combined use: in 7 post-mortem samples, sent to a laboratory because peaks suggesting cocaethylene had already been seen in them, it ran from 73 to 1447 ng/mL and exceeded cocaine in 4; among emergency-department samples, 10 of 17 that contained a cocaine breakdown product and alcohol held cocaethylene, against 1 of 14 that contained cocaine but no alcohol, and incubation tests showed that it does not form in a sample after collection. Those 7 deaths have no stated cause, no comparison deaths and no denominator, so they show presence, never cause (Jatlow et al., 1991). The three studies added here do not settle what cocaethylene contributes either: given on its own it was less potent than cocaine at matched doses, and when it is formed in the body its levels stay well below cocaine's, but no study gave it at the levels combined use produces, and none of these studies measured a heart event, a rhythm problem or any other harm.

set.plain: What happens when cocaine and alcohol are taken together? The body makes cocaethylene, a substance that forms only when both drugs are present. In a careful study where people drank alcohol an hour before cocaine was put into a vein, about 17 in every 100 parts of the cocaine dose turned into cocaethylene; it reached levels far below cocaine's, stayed in the blood longer, and did not appear at all without alcohol. In an earlier study of 8 adults who took cocaine by the nose with alcohol, heart rate was higher with both drugs than with cocaine alone, and there was roughly 13 to 15 percent more cocaine in the blood; with cocaine into a vein, that rise in cocaine was not found. People said they felt better, or more intoxicated, with both drugs than with cocaine alone, but their highest ratings did not clearly differ. When cocaethylene itself was given into a vein, it raised heart rate less than the same amount of cocaine and was cleared more slowly. Cocaethylene has been found in the blood of people who used both drugs, sometimes at higher levels than cocaine, including after deaths, but those tests cannot show what caused a death. Each study had 6 to 10 people, on a hospital ward, and none measured heart attacks or rhythm problems.
set.grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: Double-blind, within-person, random order, with objectively measured heart rate and drug levels; but participants knew the three possible conditions and alcohol is hard to mask, every test was counted as significant at .05 one-tailed across 15 measures without correction, and several results are printed without values (clinician ratings, six rating items, blood alcohol); the study card rates the risk of bias high overall. The three laboratory studies added in this round are also rated high on their cards (RoB 2): in Harris et al. (2003) the comparison with cocaine alone rests on an open, non-randomized session held 1 to 3 months later in 6 of the 10 people, and a cocaethylene tracer was present in every session; in Hart et al. (2000) the lower dose of each drug was always given before the higher, so dose is mixed with session order, and the blind held poorly at the lower doses. The 7 post-mortem samples of Jatlow et al. (1991) were sent because cocaethylene peaks had already been seen in them, with no cause of death, comparison deaths or denominator.
set.grade.domains.imprecision.note: Eight people and no intervals for the contrasts; the cocaine-exposure and feel-good results (p = .035 and .04, about .07 and .08 doubled) are fragile, and only the heart-rate result (p = .002) is large relative to its spread. The studies added in this round are of the same size (10 people, 6 of them in the comparison with cocaine alone; 6 people) and print P thresholds without intervals or effect sizes, so none of their null findings can be read as showing no difference.
set.grade.reasoning: A double-blind, within-person laboratory study with random order of conditions starts high (METHODS §6.3). Risk of bias −1: unmasked alcohol, one-tailed uncorrected tests across 15 measures and results printed without values in the first study; an unblinded comparator session in the second; a fixed ascending dose order in the third. Imprecision −2: 6 to 10 people per study, no intervals, and fragile results for cocaine exposure and feel good. Inconsistency 0: the one disagreement, whether alcohol raises blood cocaine, follows the route (found with intranasal cocaine, not with intravenous), which the authors of both studies give as the explanation. Indirectness 0 as worded. Certainty very low. Status replicated: that cocaethylene forms only when both drugs are present is found by three independent groups (McCance-Katz et al., 1998; Jatlow et al., 1991; Harris et al., 2003), and a higher heart rate with the combination than with cocaine alone in two (the second unblinded). Not counted as independent: McCance-Katz et al. (1998) and Hart et al. (2000) share investigators, and the narrative review includes the first study. The claim does not say that the effects are more than additive, and it does not say that the combination raises the chance of a heart attack or a rhythm problem, which none of the sources read measured; nor does it say what cocaethylene contributes to the combination, which no study read tests, since cocaethylene was given alone only at levels higher than combined use produces.
set.grade.domains.inconsistency.note: Four primary laboratory studies now point the same way on the formation of cocaethylene and on heart rate; the one disagreement, whether alcohol raises blood cocaine (up to 30% higher with intranasal cocaine, no difference with intravenous cocaine), follows the route of administration, which both sets of authors give as the explanation. The review's emergency-room data show no clear excess of heart problems, which the claim also says.

set.plain: Can cocaine make someone feel less drunk? In a careful laboratory study of 10 adults who drank alcohol an hour before cocaine was put into a vein, how drunk they said the alcohol made them feel was the same whether cocaine followed or not, and their breath alcohol was the same. A review of other small laboratory studies says people given cocaine with alcohol did not rate themselves as more drunk, and in three studies rated themselves slightly less drunk, though those differences were small and mostly not clearly different from chance. Cocaine also made some alcohol-affected test scores less poor. No study asked other people how drunk someone looked, or tested driving, and records of drivers who died show that some had both drugs in their blood, so the combination did not protect them from alcohol's effects.
set.verification.flag_note: No longer rests only on narrative reviews: one primary laboratory study (Harris et al., 2003) has been read in full and anchored, so the claim moves from draft to metadata-verified (METHODS §6.3, §12); its two new anchors are ai-located and need a second reader's check. The primary studies the review describes (Farre 1993 and 1997, Higgins 1993, Perez-Reyes and Jeffcoat 1992, Foltin 1993, Higgins 1992) were not read and have no reference records here. WRITING-RULES rule 0: the practical worry is that a person who feels less drunk, or is thought sober by others, takes on more risk; no source read asks other people to judge how drunk someone looks, and none tests driving. In the study read in full the alcohol was drunk an hour before the cocaine, so its peak came first.
set.grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: The primary studies cannot be appraised from the review: it gives no study-level risk-of-bias assessment, and its tables disagree with its text in places (card reporting issues). The one primary study read in full is double-blind and within-person with an objective alcohol measure, but its study card rates it high overall (an unblinded comparator session, many measures without correction), and its intoxication ratings are single unvalidated scales.
set.grade.domains.indirectness.note: Second-hand for the studies described by the review, and based throughout on self-rated drunkenness and test scores in a laboratory, not on how drunk someone appears to others or on real-world impairment. In the study read in full, alcohol was drunk an hour before the cocaine, so peak alcohol was reached before any cocaine arrived.
set.grade.domains.imprecision.note: Studies of 6 to 11 people as described by the review, and 10 in the study read in full; the review's table labels the falls in rated drunkenness non-significant, and no effect sizes are given in either source.
set.grade.reasoning: The claim now rests on one primary double-blind, placebo-controlled laboratory study read in full (which starts high, METHODS §6.3) together with a narrative review's second-hand account of 14 further laboratory studies. Risk of bias −1: the primary studies in the review cannot be appraised from it, its tables disagree with its text in places, and in the study read in full the ratings are single unvalidated scales spoken or typed by participants. Indirectness −1: self-rated drunkenness and task scores in a laboratory, not how drunk a person appears to others or what they can do outside; and in the study read in full the alcohol was drunk an hour before the cocaine, so its peak came before any cocaine arrived, which is not the order in which people usually combine them, by the review's account. Imprecision −1: 6 to 11 people in the studies the review describes, 10 in the study read in full, with the review's table labelling the falls in rated drunkenness non-significant and no effect sizes given anywhere. Certainty very low. Status replicated: the direction, no increase in rated drunkenness when cocaine is added to alcohol, is found in one primary study read in full and in four studies whose direction the review reports, from independent groups; the sizes are not established, and the review's description of at least one study it covers is inaccurate (study card). The roadside-fatality figures are context: they show that people who had taken both drugs were not protected from alcohol's effects, not whether they looked less drunk.

evidence_add.extracted: The study reports no rating of drunkenness separate from the alcohol-intoxication rating; its other ratings are of cocaine intoxication, total intoxication, drug liking and good drug effect, which rose with the cocaine dose. In the 6 of 10 people who also had a cocaine-alone session, total intoxication and drug liking across time were higher with alcohol, in a session that was neither blinded nor randomized. The authors note that the absence of any difference in peak alcohol levels and effects with cocaine added is what would be expected when the alcohol is drunk an hour beforehand, and that another study found no difference in blood alcohol or rated alcohol intoxication when cocaine was given before the alcohol.
